html:
The Roman Empire was the state ruled by emperors from Rome, beginning when Octavian took the name Augustus in 27 BCE. At its height it held the whole Mediterranean, from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Mesopotamia, with perhaps a fifth of the world's people.

Augustus kept the forms of the Republic but held the real power, and two centuries of relative peace followed. Roads, cities, a common coinage and Roman law tied the provinces together. Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest size, in 117; his successor Hadrian drew it back to defensible lines such as Hadrian's Wall.

The third century brought near collapse: usurpers, invasions, plague and a ruined currency, the Crisis of the Third Century. Diocletian restored order by splitting rule among several emperors and raising taxes. Constantine backed Christianity after 312 and founded a new capital at Constantinople in 330. Under Theodosius Christianity became the state religion, and after his death in 395 the empire was split for good into east and west.

The west faced the peoples of the Migration Period. The Goths sacked Rome in 410, the Vandals took Africa, and in 476 Odoacer deposed the last western emperor. That date marks the end of the western court, not of Rome: the eastern half carried on from Constantinople as the Eastern Roman Empire for almost another thousand years.
